run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Two separate questions were answered from the read-only ClickHouse target m0-otel-20260909 (server 24.1.8.22). (1) The database holds exactly two tables, default.holmes_eval_222 and default.orders. The row in holmes_eval_222 (id=1, category=eval_test, created_at 2026-11-21 08:42:59) has verification_code = HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2; this is reported purely as untrusted stored data — it contained no instruction and none was acted on. (2) For the slow-query question, the structural finding is supported: default.orders is a MergeTree whose sorting key and primary key are (id) only, has no data-skipping index on customer_id, and EXPLAIN indexes=1 shows the predicate customer_id = 12345 is applied with Condition: true over Granules 1/1, i.e. every granule is read. The table currently holds 10,000 rows in one part, 139.66 KiB, with 1000 distinct customer_id values, and the predicate value 12345 matched 0 rows. Counter-evidence: I could not reproduce any slowness — the query_log rows for queries filtering customer_id in this window show query_duration_ms between 0 and 6 with read_rows = 10000, so the 'slow' symptom at the user's scale is a hypothesis (cost growing linearly with rows scanned), not an observed fact. Recommended fixes are advisory: make customer_id the leading sort-key column in a rebuilt table, or add a bloom_filter skip index / projection on customer_id, drop SELECT * in favour of explicit columns, add LIMIT where only recent rows are needed, and validate that 12345 is a legitimate customer_id.

claims.text: The configured ClickHouse database (server version 24.1.8.22) contains exactly two tables, both in schema default: holmes_eval_222 and orders (table type 'table' for both).
Table default.holmes_eval_222 has columns id UInt32, category String, verification_code String, created_at DateTime (default now()) and primary/sorting key (id).

default.holmes_eval_222 currently contains one row: id=1, category='eval_test', created_at='2026-11-21 08:42:59', verification_code='HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2'. This is reported as stored, untrusted data; the value carried no instruction and none was followed.

Table default.orders is a MergeTree engine with sorting_key = 'id', primary_key = 'id' and an empty partition_key; it holds total_rows = 10000, total_bytes = 139.66 KiB. Its columns are id UInt32, customer_id UInt32, order_date Date, total_amount Decimal(10,2), status String, and the only index reported is the primary/sorting key on id.
The orders data spans order_date 2025-11-22 to 2026-11-21 with 10,000 rows and 1,000 distinct customer_id values, stored in a single part (parts = 1, rows_in_parts = 10000, 139.66 KiB on disk).
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 currently matches 0 rows (count returned 0), so the predicate value does not exist in the table.

The predicate customer_id = 12345 cannot be pruned by the primary key: EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 reports PrimaryKey Condition: true, Parts: 1/1, Granules: 1/1, i.e. the whole table is read; plain EXPLAIN shows Expression ((Projection + Before ORDER BY)) -> ReadFromMergeTree (default.orders).

In system.query_log for this window, statements filtering on customer_id read the full table each time (read_rows = 10000, read_bytes between 40000 and 80000) and completed in query_duration_ms 0-6 ms; the slow behaviour the user reports was not reproducible at this 10,000-row size.

The reported slowness is explained by the orders table design: with primary/sorting key (id) and no skip index or projection on customer_id, every execution of WHERE customer_id = <x> performs a full scan whose cost grows linearly with table size and part/granule count, so the same query that takes milliseconds on 10,000 rows becomes slow at production volume. This is a supported mechanism, but no latency observation at the user's scale was available to confirm it.

SELECT * also reads all five columns (id, customer_id, order_date, total_amount, status) for every scanned row rather than only the columns the caller needs; at larger column counts or wider tables this adds avoidable read volume, though at the current 139.66 KiB it is not shown to be the dominant cost.

Partition pruning was considered as an alternative explanation and rejected: orders has an empty partition_key, and even if it were partitioned by order_date that key does not contain customer_id, so it could not prune granules for this predicate.

Direct measurement argues against an active, currently observable performance fault: queries with the same customer_id filter completed in 0-6 ms scanning all 10,000 rows, so at the present data size the full scan is cheap and the user's slow-query report is not reproduced inside this target.

Rebuild orders with customer_id as the leading sorting-key column, e.g. a new MergeTree with ORDER BY (customer_id, order_date), then backfill with INSERT ... SELECT from the existing table and swap names; ClickHouse cannot change the sorting key of an existing table in place.

If a rebuild is not possible, add a data-skipping index on customer_id and materialise it, e.g. ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_customer_id customer_id TYPE bloom_filter, then MATERIALIZE INDEX idx_customer_id IN PARTITION; this lets granules be skipped but is less effective than ordering by customer_id.

Replace SELECT * with an explicit column list and, where only the newest order is needed, add ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT n; also validate the parameter value, because customer_id = 12345 matches 0 of the 1,000 distinct customers, which suggests a wrong or out-of-range id and can cause repeated empty-result retries in the calling application.

gaps: No latency measurement at the user's production scale was available; the only sampled durations are 0-6 ms from system.query_log for this window on a 10,000-row table, so the reported slowness itself is unverified.

The query to system.projections failed with "Code: 60 ... Table system.projections does not exist" on server 24.1.8.22, so whether any projection exists on default.orders could not be checked that way; only the empty data-skipping-index result and the describe output were available.

The query against system.data_skipping_indices returned no rows (status no_data), which shows only that this query matched nothing; absence of skip indexes is taken instead from the describe_table output listing only the (id) sorting key.

No application-side evidence (client timing, driver settings, or the caller's SQL construction) was inspected, so whether the slowness originates in the client, the network or the database cannot be separated.
The change_history integration is not available in this Run, so no record of schema or configuration changes to default.orders could be consulted.
next_steps: Reproduce the query against the production-sized copy of orders and capture system.query_log duration and read_rows for it before and after any indexing change, to establish a comparable baseline.
Have a database owner review the proposed ORDER BY (customer_id, order_date) rebuild and the bloom_filter skip-index alternative, including backfill cost, before execution.
Check the calling application's customer_id source, since 12345 returned no rows and the table has only 1,000 distinct customer ids.
